newsitem.title: FINLAND: Regional merger not seen near for Merita.
newsitem.headline: Regional merger not seen near for Merita.

text.p: Sharp recent gains in Finnish banking group Merita's stock stem more from broker ratings and target prices for the share than from genuine speculation on a regional merger, analysts say.
"I don't see that Merita has a great deal to achieve from merging with a Scandinavian bank," said Ian McEwan, analyst at Lehman Brothers in London.
Recent gains in Merita, which some brokers have attributed to talk of more consolidation in the Nordic financial sector, have set the pace for the Helsinki financials subindex.

Both Merita and the index have gained well over 60 percent this year, with Merita up 50 percent in the past five weeks from a June 19 trough of 16.20. At Friday midsession Merita's stock was up 0.30 markka at a new year-high of 24.60.

Much of the speculation has focused on Nordic merger scenarios, with Swedish SE Banken reported to have been close to a deal with state-controlled Nordbanken in May, and a planned merger between Norwegian insurer Storebrand ASA and Christiania Bank blocked last month.

But analysts said a cross-border merger with Merita was unlikely soon, not only because of its size -- with $50 billion assets, it is the fifth largest financial services provider in the Nordic area -- but also because it would yield few benefits.

"I am sure the Swedes would be interested in cooperation, not least in marketing their mutual funds, but going as far as an acquisition (of Merita) is not likely," said Ingemar Persson, banking analyst at Aros in Oslo.
Created by a 1995 merger of the then-leading banks Unitas and KOP, Merita is Finland's biggest bank with over 40 percent of the country's deposits and 43 percent of lending.
It said in February it had talked to major Finnish insurers Sampo and Pohjola about cooperation last year, but that the talks came to nothing.
Mundane as it seems, analysts say recent recommendations on the share from the likes of Goldman Sachs, Lehman Brothers and SE Banken explain overseas demand.
Goldman started Merita as a market outperformer on June 30, and Lehman has had a buy on it since March.
"Recommendations from a few big foreign houses are enough to explain the interest in the share," said Jussi Hyoty of AG Private Bankers.
Competition restrictions could rule out mergers between the big three in Finnish banking and insurance -- Merita, Pohjola and Sampo -- analysts added.

"For cartel reasons it would be difficult to put any two of the three together because you would then have a massive force that might not be acceptable without a balancing force," said Giovanni Govi of Goldman Sachs in London.

There has also been loose talk of a share issue to replace the bank's debt to the state, but some analysts say the state-held capital notes are cheap capital and the rumours do not explain the share's rise.

Rather than Merita, Finland's big insurers could be interested in cross-border mergers as a defensive measure, analysts said. "Otherwise they might fall prey to the Allianzs, Zurichs and INGs of the world," said Govi.
But analysts agreed last week's German merger of Bavarian Vereinsbank AG and Hypo-Bank does show more general consolidation ahead.
"It shows that the playing field is being put into shape for European economic and monetary union," Hyoty said.
